newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan insurers altering U.S. bond strategy - traders.
newsitem.headline: Japan insurers altering U.S. bond strategy - traders.

text.p: Japanese life insurers have altered their traditional investment strategy of holding on to U.S. bonds for the long term and are starting to sell them for quick profits on dollar rallies, traders said on Friday.

They said that insurers are growing more concerned about the risk of currency fluctuations and have become more willing to offload some of their U.S. bond holdings when the dollar rises against the yen for quick forex gains.

The insurers' new investment stance is in clear contrast to Japanese pension and public funds, which tend to step up foreign bond buying when the dollar firms, said a senior fund manager at a life insurance firm.
"There should be more chances to bargain-hunt (the dollar) later after this round of buying is over," a fund manager at a another major insurer said.
While, another insurer's fund manager said: "We'll maintain our stance of buying the dollar on falls, and not on rallies. Many life insurers may have a similar strategy."

The insurers say they are expecting the dollar to head towards the 125-yen level from April. But the longer term dollar trend is uncertain, which should make insurers reluctant to buy aggressively on rallies.

"People are not as bullish about the dollar now as they were in December," the first manager said. "As long as the outlook for the dollar is unclear, the insurers will be very careful about extending their foreign bond investments."

Traders said Japanese insurers have been building up their foreign bond holdings in recent years on the dollar's recovery from the April 1995 low of about 80 yen, and also because of super-low interest rates at home.
Foreign bond investments by Japanese investors are made in U.S. dollars because of the currency's high liquidity. Any appreciation of the dollar would result in income gains for dollar-based bonds.
In the early 1990s Japanese investors, particularly life insurers, reduced their foreign bond investments after their profits were battered by the yen's appreciation.
Market sources estimate that insurers' foreign bond holdings are now equal to about five to six percent of their total assets, compared with about 20 percent during the peak levels of the 1980s.

"Past experience has taught life insurers to be more careful, especially after their profits were severely battered by the sharp appreciation of the yen. The insurers are trying not to buy dollars at high levels now," the first fund manager said.
Other fund managers said they will adopt a cautious stance and refrain from buying bonds aggressively from the start of the new fiscal year in April.
"I think the investors who have been building up their foreign bond holdings may be less aggressive from the start of the year," the third fund manager said.
